title: Pachomius' community
hookLine: monks living together under a rule: work, prayer, shared bread

lines: A RECRUIT, LOCKED UP AND HUNGRY.
cards: Locked up with other recruits in a city on the Nile, rounded up for the emperor's army, sits a young man who isn't a Christian. He's hungry and far from home.
In the evening, strangers come with food and drink for the prisoners. He asks who they are. Christians, he's told: people who are kind to strangers, for the sake of the God of heaven.
His name is Pachomius. His Life says that night he promised that, if he got free, he would spend his life serving others. A few days ago, Antony walked out alone into the desert.
Pachomius goes too, but he doesn't stay alone.

teach.b: After his release, Pachomius is baptized and learns the hard life of a hermit from an old monk.
Then, at a deserted village by the river called Tabennesi, the story goes, he's told to build a place where many could live together. So he does, and it gets hard.

His first followers, the Life says, took advantage of him. He served them, cooked, did the chores, and they treated him like the help. He gave them a rule, and when they wouldn't keep it, he sent them away.
Living together was harder than living alone. So Pachomius organized it.
Monks lived in houses, each with a leader. They worked with their hands, weaving mats and baskets, and the work supported the community and the poor.
They prayed at set times and ate together, the same food at a shared table. The sick were cared for. Nobody owned anything privately.
People kept coming, and more communities were founded along the river.
Acts had already described this way of life among the first Christians in Jerusalem: "they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."

The Greek word behind fellowship there is koinonia, a life held in common, and Pachomius' communities came to be called by that name: the Koinonia. Alone in a cave, nobody leaves dishes in your sink. Nobody snores.
Nobody needs you when you're tired. In community, everyone does. As the Life tells it, for Pachomius that was the point.

how: Christian monks and nuns in Orthodox, Catholic and other traditions live in community under a rule, sharing work, prayer at set hours, and meals.

o: monks sharing work, prayer and bread under one rule
a camp on the Nile for the emperor's new recruits
a hermit living alone in a cave out in the desert

p: a deserted village by the river

s: Pachomius became a Christian because soldiers preached to him
Christians brought food to the hungry recruits. that's what moved him.
his first followers made life easy for him
the Life says they took advantage of him, and he sent them away.
the monks ate together at a shared table
work, prayer and bread, held in common.

games.q: you're Pachomius. your first followers treat you like a servant and ignore the rule. what do you do?
o: give up and go back to living alone.
keep serving them and never say a word.
send them away, and build again with a rule.
games.why: the Life says he sent them away, and the community he built after them grew.

practice: Bring to mind the people you share space or work with, and notice the small friction points, the dishes, the trash, the one always late, without stewing.

Then pick one chore that usually falls to one person and imagine doing it alongside them, not instead of them, the way Pachomius' monks shared the work and the bread. If you pray, pray for the people you live with, by name.

wordCard.voice: Pachomius' community. The shared life Pachomius built by the Nile: houses of monks under a rule, with work, prayer and bread held in common.

orig.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing, a life in common. the word in Acts 2:42, and the name of Pachomius' communities.

carryVoice: Your line: together is harder, and better. The dishes are part of it. Until next time.
